report.source_text: Examination of the feet revealed a distinct boundary between normal skin and affected crusted skin overlying osteolysis (“split” sign) on the third toe involving circumferentially the entire toe (Fig. 1). It was slightly painful and associated with serous discharge but no discharge of the bony spicules. Additionally, there was a shortening of the distal phalanx of the second, fourth, and fifth toes. The sensation and peripheral pulses of the feet were normal.

report.source_text: Laboratory investigations that included complete blood count, renal function tests, liver function tests, parathyroid hormone, anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP test, C-reactive protein, fasting blood sugar, serum calcium, inorganic phosphate, albumin, and thyroid function tests were in normal ranges. This workup helped rule out infections, e.g., osteomyelitis, connective tissue, endocrine, and lipid storage disease. There were no clinical or radiographic findings of inflammatory/rheumatic disorders such as psoriatic arthritis.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 5-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of a transverse cutaneous 'split' on the plantar aspect of the right third toe with serous discharge that elongated circumferentially within 1 month, accompanied by shortening of the distal phalanges of the 2nd, 4th, and 5th toes. The mother also had similar transient lesions with toe shortening. Clinical examination revealed a distinct boundary between normal and crusted skin (split sign) and signs of osteolysis. Radiologic imaging (X-rays) during early workup confirmed complete and partial resorption of multiple distal phalanges. Laboratory investigations were normal, ruling out infectious, inflammatory, endocrine, and connective tissue disorders. Histopathologic examination was ordered but no results were documented. No clinical course or treatment response data were available.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Distinct boundary ('split' sign) between normal skin and crusted skin overlying osteolysis on the third toe
X-rays demonstrating complete and partial resorption of distal phalanges of several toes consistent with osteolysis
Normal laboratory tests ruling out infections, inflammatory, endocrine, and connective tissue disorders
History of similar lesions and phalangeal shortening in the patient's mother supporting hereditary or idiopathic etiology
